chapter_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Meeting the Poem: Read-Aloud and First Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp.67–68): read poem aloud; attend to new words.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the chapter title. Ask children what activities keep them healthy and happy, drawing a quick shared list on the board. This opens the poem's world without reading it yet.

Let us Read (pp.67–68): Read the poem aloud expressively, once all the way through, then a second time with children echoing each triplet or couplet. Pause on new words — mistakes, proudly, pace, rhythm, cheerful, swift — pointing to them in the text and giving brief meanings in context.
Invite children to re-read along silently while you read a third time at a moderate pace. Ask two or three volunteers to read a stanza each, supporting their pronunciation warmly.
Close by asking: 'Which child in the poem are you most like, and why?' Take three or four quick responses. No written work; oral sharing only.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem has five named children, each introduced with an alliterative quality-descriptor — 'Active Anant', 'Graceful Geeta', and so on. Lingering on those descriptors during the read-aloud plants the seed for the adjective work that follows in later word-work units. Keep the new-word explanations brisk and contextual rather than dictionary-style; the children need the meanings to track the poem, not to memorise definitions.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.69): discuss four comprehension questions about the poem.

time_bands.activity: Begin with a quick choral recitation of the poem (pp.67–68). The whole class recites together once, with the teacher keeping a gentle rhythm by tapping the desk. This refreshes the text in children's minds before the discussion.

Let us Think B (p.69): pose the first two comprehension questions — which game Anant plays, and which musical instruments appear in the poem — as a pair-share. Each child tells their partner the answer, then the class shares. Record key answers briefly on the board.

Continue with the third and fourth questions — who moves in rhythm, and who learns from skating mistakes. Children respond individually in full oral sentences; model a complete sentence answer before asking them. Gently correct sentence structure rather than content.
Children write their answers to all four questions in their notebooks in complete sentences. Teacher circulates and reads a few responses aloud as positive examples.

periods.teacher_notes: Guitar and sitar both appear in the Lhamo stanza; children may name only one instrument — prompt them to look at the stanza again. The question about rhythm points specifically to Meena; if children say 'Lhamo' redirect them by rereading the final named stanza together.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss: Sport, Music, and Dance

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think C (p.69): guided discussion on games, instruments, and dance.

time_bands.activity: Open with the poem's closing lines — 'Cheerful children everywhere, / playing is a joy! / for every girl and boy.' Ask children to say those lines together and then explain in one word what those lines are celebrating. Collect three or four responses.

Let us Think C (p.69), questions 1–2: children turn to a partner and discuss which game they play in school and whether they prefer indoor or outdoor games. After two minutes of pair talk, selected children share with the class; teacher models a comparison sentence ('I enjoy outdoor games more because…').

Let us Think C (p.69), questions 3–4: whole-class discussion on musical instruments. Children name instruments they have seen or played; the teacher lists them on the board, noticing any that appear in the poem (guitar, sitar). Celebrate diversity of responses.

Let us Think C (p.69), question 5: each child names a dance form they like and, if they can, a famous dance from their region. Pair-share first, then a few children present to the class in one or two sentences. Teacher acknowledges regional diversity warmly.

periods.teacher_notes: Children may struggle to name a regional dance; accepting descriptive answers ('the dance we do at our festival') is valid — the goal is confident oral expression. Keep the board list of instruments visible; it connects the poem's guitar and sitar to the children's real-world knowledge.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Alliterative Adjectives: What Quality Describes You?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.69): write one alliterative quality matching your own name.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the poem's five named children and their descriptors on the board: Active Anant, Graceful Geeta, Little Lhamo, Swift Shabana, Musical Meena. Ask children what all the descriptors have in common with the names. Guide them to notice that each describing word starts with the same letter as the name — introduce the term 'alliteration' briefly.

Let us Think A (p.69): children think of one quality (adjective) that starts with the same first letter as their own name, following the poem's pattern. Invite volunteers to say their phrase aloud — model one or two with the teacher's own name first. Children then write their phrase in their notebook.

Share-out: go around the room quickly — each child says their alliterative phrase in a full sentence: 'I am Brave Bhavna.' Celebrate variety, correct gently if the word chosen is not an adjective. Build a class poem by writing two or three of the best phrases on the board as a short list.
Quick reflection: ask 'Is 'Active' a naming word or a describing word?' and 'How does adding 'Active' change what you know about Anant?' Take three responses to consolidate what an adjective does.

periods.teacher_notes: Children may choose generic qualities like 'good' or 'nice'; gently redirect them to more vivid adjectives by giving quick synonyms ('brave, cheerful, curious, daring…'). The alliterative pattern is the poem's dominant device and is worth spending time on — it anchors the formal adjective lesson that follows.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Adjectives in Action: Matching and Noun-Pairing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.70): match adjectives to correct nouns.
Let us Learn B (p.70): fill blanks with suitable nouns and adjectives.

time_bands.activity: Write two phrases from the poem on the board: 'rocky ground' and 'fastest pace'. Ask: which word is the adjective and which is the noun? Invite three quick responses to reinforce the concept from the alliterative adjectives work. Briefly restate: an adjective tells us more about a noun.

Let us Learn A (p.70): children complete the matching task in their notebooks — blue/sky, hardworking/children, green/vegetables, pebbled/road, healthy/leaves (correct pairs per the exercise). Teacher reads each adjective aloud and children suggest the match before writing. Discuss why 'pebbled' fits 'road' but not 'sky'.

Let us Learn B (p.70): first half — adjective given, children supply a noun (happy ___, red ___, fierce ___, beautiful ___). Accept multiple correct answers. Then second half — noun given, children supply an adjective (___ mangoes, ___ baby, ___ nation, ___ winner). Elicit varied responses, noting that many adjectives can fit.
Rapid oral round: teacher points to classroom objects and children race to give an adjective for each. Closes the concept playfully and revisits today's grammar in a spoken register.

periods.teacher_notes: The matching task has a built-in answer key in the textbook; circulate to check that children are writing the pairs in both directions (adjective → noun) rather than just copying. For the fill-in half, open-ended answers are valid — mark any grammatically correct and contextually plausible pairing as correct.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Double-Letter Words: Picture Prompt and Guided Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p.71): fill blanks with double-letter words using the parrot picture.

homework.task_brief: Let us Write B (p.71): find five kitchen items whose spellings contain double letters and list them.

time_bands.activity: Write the word 'village' on the board and underline 'll'. Ask children to find the double letters. Then brainstorm together: what other words have double letters? Accept all responses and circle the doubled letters on the board (bell, egg, happy, parrot, coffee).

Let us Write A (p.71): children look at the picture of the parrot in the textbook. Read the sentence frame aloud together: 'This is my pet ___. It loves to eat ___, which are ___ in colour.' Children discuss in pairs what words with double letters could fill each blank (parrot, berries/apples, green/yellow). Take suggestions and note them on the board.

Children write the complete three-sentence passage in their notebooks, choosing their best double-letter words. Teacher circulates, prompting children who are stuck by writing the first letter of the target word on their page as a clue. A few children read their completed sentences aloud.
Quick class check: teacher reads aloud one correct version for each blank and children confirm or correct their own work. Highlight the double letters in the solutions on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The picture shows a parrot, so 'parrot' (double r) is the intended answer for the first blank; 'berries' or 'seeds' work for the second; 'green' or 'yellow' for the third. Accept any grammatically sensible double-letter word — the device focus is spelling pattern, not a single right answer. The homework asks children to search their kitchen at home; it is deliberate real-world vocabulary discovery.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Rhyming Words: Finding Patterns in the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write C (p.72): find and write rhyming words from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Read the Anant stanza aloud — 'Active boy Anant, / plays the game of hockey, / even when the ground is rocky.' Ask: which two words sound alike? Establish 'hockey' and 'rocky' as a rhyming pair and write them on the board. Briefly define rhyming words: words that share the same ending sound.

Let us Write C (p.72): children open to the poem and find the rhyming pair for 'hockey'. Confirm. Then, working in pairs, they scan the poem to find the rhyming partners for 'skates', 'guitar', 'race', and 'joy'. Teacher circulates and supports those who struggle to identify 'sitar' as the partner for 'guitar'.

Class check: teacher reads each prompt word and children call out the partner. Record all five pairs on the board: hockey/rocky, skates/mistakes, guitar/sitar, race/pace, joy/boy. Children copy the pairs in their notebooks and underline the shared sound pattern in each pair.
Extension challenge: children try to add one more word of their own that rhymes with any pair (e.g. 'stocking' for hockey/rocky). Take four or five responses orally. Celebrate creative additions.

periods.teacher_notes: The rhyming pair 'guitar/sitar' may be unfamiliar in sound to some children — model the pronunciation of both words before they search. 'Joy/boy' spans stanzas, so some children may overlook it; direct them to the closing lines of the poem.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Word Meanings: Matching Definitions to Poem Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write D (p.72): match five poem words to their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Write the five target words on the board: Brave, Rocky, Mistakes, Proudly, Delightful. Ask children to use the poem's context to guess the meaning of each word before consulting any source. Take quick estimates and note them on the board without confirming.

Let us Write D (p.72): read each definition aloud from the textbook, one at a time, and ask children to decide which word matches. They write their answer in the circle space (or in their notebook). Work through all five definitions as a class, verifying by returning to the poem context where useful.

Children use each of the five words in an original spoken sentence. Teacher models one: 'The cheerful children played proudly on the rocky ground.' Invite children to compose their own, correcting meaning use gently rather than form.

Quick written consolidation: children copy the five words and write a two-word phrase of their own using each (e.g. 'brave soldier', 'rocky path'). This reinforces the adjective work from the matching activity done earlier in the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: 'Proudly' and 'delightful' are the two words most likely to be confused — 'proudly' describes the manner of doing something, while 'delightful' describes the quality of a thing or experience. Use the poem's line 'proudly plays a guitar' to anchor the distinction. The written phrase task at the close connects naturally to the adjective-noun pairing work.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: No-Fire Cooking Activity: Healthy Food, Healthy Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.71): organise a 'Preparing a Dish Without Fire' class activity.

time_bands.activity: Connect to the poem's theme — a fit body needs both activity AND healthy food. Ask children: 'Can you prepare something healthy without using any fire or stove?' Take suggestions (fruit salad, sandwiches, salads). Briefly explain the activity: each small group will prepare and present a no-fire dish.

Let us Do (p.71): children work in groups of four or five to prepare their dish using ingredients brought to class or provided by the teacher (fruit, bread, vegetables, yoghurt, etc.). Each group also prepares a one- or two-sentence description of why their dish is healthy. Teacher circulates and assists.

Each group presents their dish to the class and reads their health description aloud. The class listens and asks one question per group ('What ingredient makes it healthy?'). Teacher leads a brief tasting if hygiene conditions allow.
Wrap up with the poem's closing message: healthy food and joyful play together make a fit nation. Children repeat the final two lines of the poem together.

periods.teacher_notes: Coordinate with school administration in advance for permission to bring ingredients. If preparation is not feasible, pivot to a planning activity: each group designs their dish on paper, names its healthy ingredients, and presents the plan orally. The activity's oral presentation component ties directly to the chapter's oracy strand.

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore (p.72): find out about the Paralympic Games and share with the class.

time_bands.activity: Ask children: 'Have you heard of the Olympic Games? Are there games for athletes who have a physical disability?' Take responses freely and write the word 'Paralympic' on the board. Ask what the prefix 'Para' might mean and record guesses without confirming yet.

Let us Explore (p.72): provide children with a brief teacher-prepared fact sheet (or read aloud from a prepared note) about the Paralympic Games — what they are, when they started, which sports feature, and how they connect to the poem's theme of sport and fitness for everyone. Children take three key points in their notebooks.

Children work in pairs to prepare a short two-sentence share-out: one fact about the Paralympics and one personal reaction ('I found it amazing that…'). Each pair presents to the class. Teacher adds one connecting thought after each pair.

Connect back to the poem: the poem says 'playing is a joy for every girl and boy' — discuss how the Paralympics embodies exactly this idea. Children say in one spoken sentence how the poem and the Paralympics are connected.

periods.teacher_notes: A simple teacher-prepared fact sheet prevents the lesson from depending on internet access. Key facts to include: the Paralympics began in 1960, run alongside the Olympics, feature sports such as wheelchair racing, sitting volleyball, and blind football. The connection to the poem's inclusive closing lines ('for every girl and boy') makes this a genuine extension of the poem's theme, not a detached project.
materials: Teacher-prepared fact sheet on Paralympic Games

periods.section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
periods.activity_title: Bringing It All Together: Poem, Words, and Our Voices

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-class choral reading of the poem (pp.67–68). Each group takes one named child's stanza and the class reads the closing lines together. The teacher leads with a steady rhythm, inviting children to clap the beat.

Quick word-work round: teacher calls out a definition — from the vocabulary work on words such as 'proudly', 'swift', 'cheerful', 'pace', and 'rocky' — and children race to write the matching word on a small slip of paper and hold it up. Three or four rounds, covering both poem vocabulary and adjective knowledge.

Each child writes two sentences in their notebook: a new alliterative phrase for themselves (following the 'Active Anant' pattern) and one sentence using that adjective to describe something in the poem's spirit — fitness, joy, or talent. This brief independent writing task begins and closes within these minutes.

Recitation and beyond-text close: children take turns performing their own alliterative line aloud ('Curious Chetan plays cricket…'). The class echoes each line once. Then, collectively, compose a final couplet that could follow the poem's closing — 'Cheerful children everywhere…' — accepting two or three suggestions and choosing one to write on the board.

Final choral recitation of the whole poem one more time, with the new class-composed couplet added at the end. Teacher celebrates the chapter's journey: reading, talking, playing with words, writing, cooking, and exploring sport.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together the alliterative adjective concept, the poem's vocabulary, the rhyme patterns, and the poem's inclusive spirit — all of which the chapter explored across its reading, word-work, oracy, writing, and beyond-text strands. The independent writing task is compact by design so that it opens and completes within the minutes available. The class-composed couplet is a genuine creative outcome that belongs to this sitting alone.
materials: Small paper slips for word-work round

items.source_section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
items.source_lo: Student reads and retrieves explicit information using a celebratory poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five named children — Anant, Geeta, Lhamo, Shabana, Meena — each with alliterative descriptors; sports, musical instruments, rhythm.
items.item_stem: Look at the poem on pages 67–68. Which sport does Anant play, and what does Geeta learn from doing every day?

options.label: A
options.text: Anant plays cricket; Geeta learns from practising yoga every day.

options.label: B
options.text: Anant plays hockey; Geeta learns from her mistakes in skating every day.

options.label: C
options.text: Anant plays football; Geeta learns from cycling faster every day.

options.label: D
options.text: Anant plays hockey; Geeta learns from watching Lhamo play guitar every day.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child knows Anant plays hockey but has confused Geeta's activity with an unrelated one.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has confused Anant's sport with a different outdoor game and misread Geeta's stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child correctly identifies Anant's sport but conflates Geeta's learning with Lhamo's stanza.

items.item_stem: The poem on pages 67–68 introduces Meena and Shabana differently — one celebrates a victory and the other sings. In your own words, write one sentence saying what Shabana did to celebrate and one sentence saying how Meena expresses herself.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Shabana won a cycle race and happily celebrated her fastest pace. Meena expresses herself by singing in rhythm.

items.source_section_title: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
items.source_lo: Student expresses personal experience and preference in spoken English using a poem as the stimulus.
items.source_context: Games, indoor vs outdoor play, musical instruments, regional dance forms; prompted by the poem's five children.
items.item_stem:
The poem shows five children enjoying different activities — hockey, skating, guitar, cycle racing, and singing. Listen to these two statements and decide which one is TRUE.
1. The poem says that only outdoor sports make children cheerful.
2. The poem says that playing is a joy for every girl and boy.

options.text: The poem says that only outdoor sports make children cheerful.
The poem says that playing is a joy for every girl and boy.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is false — the poem celebrates both sports and music, including indoor music-making. Statement 2 is true — the closing lines read 'playing is a joy! for every girl and boy.'

items.source_context: Games, indoor vs outdoor play, musical instruments, regional dance forms; prompted by the poem's five children.
items.item_stem: The poem celebrates every child's unique talent — hockey, skating, music, cycling, and singing. If you were one of the five children in the poem, which one would you be and why? Speak two or three sentences to your teacher.

expected_elements: Names one child from the poem by name.
States a personal reason connected to an activity.
Speaks in complete sentences with reasonable fluency.

items.item_stem:
Choose the correct word to complete each sentence. The missing words all have double letters in their spelling.

1. The ___ sat on the branch and called out loudly. (parrot / pigeon)
2. The fruit was ___ in colour. (green / yellow)
3. She put the food in a ___ bowl. (small / large)

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. parrot (double r). 2. yellow (double l). 3. small (double l).
